questions.text:
const list = { 0: 1, 1: 2, length: 2 };
console.log(Array.prototype.reduce.call(list, (acc, n) => acc + n, 0));
What happens with two binds and two different objects?
options: The second bind’s this wins
this comes from the first bind. The second bind can only prepend arguments
Both objects are merged into one this
The function loses this and throws when called

questions.text: A constructor returns a value. What does new produce?
options: An object from return replaces the new this. A number or other primitive is ignored
Any return replaces this, including a number
A return from a constructor is always ignored
return is allowed only for undefined

questions.text: How do fn.call(null) and fn.call(1) differ in strict mode from sloppy mode?
options: They do not: null always becomes globalThis
In strict mode null and 1 stay as this. In sloppy mode null and undefined become the global object, and a number is boxed
In strict mode both calls throw TypeError immediately
call ignores its first argument in strict mode

questions.text: Where does this come from in a default-parameter expression?
options: From the global object: parameters are evaluated before the call
From the this of that same call. The expression runs only when the argument was omitted
Parameters have no this, so the expression always sees undefined
From the this of the previous call to this function

questions.text: A second bind can change the this fixed by the first one.
An arrow can be called with new.
If a constructor returns an object, new yields that object rather than the created this.
In strict mode fn.call(1) gets this equal to the number 1, with no Number wrapper.
Why does a getter taken from a descriptor no longer read the original object?
questions.answer: A getter is an ordinary function. obj.next calls it with this set to obj. A bare call takes this from the new call site.

questions.text: How does Function.prototype.call.call(fn, obj, arg) work?
questions.answer: call expects a callable as its own this. The outer call puts fn in that slot, the next argument becomes this for fn, and the rest are fn’s arguments.

questions.text: Why can a default value this.n throw before the function body runs?
questions.answer: The parameter expression runs at the call and uses that call’s this. A bare strict call has this === undefined, so reading this.n throws TypeError.

questions.text: Why can’t a derived constructor read this before super()?
questions.answer: Until super() returns, the base constructor has not created the instance. In a derived class, this exists only after super().

questions.text: Why does a constructor check new.target?
options: To tell whether the function was called with new or as an ordinary call
To get the this of the calling method
To forbid bind
new.target is the constructor's first argument

questions.text: Why can a class not be called through call, while an ordinary constructor function can?
options: A class has no this
A class constructor can be invoked only with new. An ordinary function accepts both call and new
call on a class silently creates an instance
An ordinary function cannot be called through call either

questions.text: Which object does an inherited getter see?
options: The prototype where the getter was declared
The object through which the property was read
Always globalThis
A getter has no this

questions.text: When do derived fields write to this, relative to the base constructor?
options: Before super(), so the base constructor already sees the derived fields
After the base constructor returns from super(), and they can overwrite what the base wrote to this
Derived fields write to a separate object, not the base this
At the same time as the first line of the base constructor

questions.text: new.target is set when the function is called with new.
After const show = Box.show, a static Box.show still sees Box as this.
An inherited getter uses the prototype itself as this, not the object through which it was read.
A private field can be read through call on any object.
What does new.target tell you?
questions.answer: Whether the function was called with new. On an ordinary call new.target is empty. With new it is the constructor written after new.

questions.text: Why does a static method pulled off the class lose the class?
questions.answer: Box.show() passes the class as this. const show = Box.show copies the function, and a bare show() no longer has the class to the left of the dot.

questions.text: Why does read.call(anotherObject) throw on a private field?
questions.answer: A private field is tied to the class instance, not to an arbitrary this. call can substitute another object, but that object has no #n to read.

questions.text: When do derived fields overwrite this.n written by the base constructor?
questions.answer: Right after super() returns, before the derived constructor body. The base writes this first, then the derived field initializers write over it.
